title: Nero Didn't Fiddle While Rome Burned #shorts
description:
Nero fiddling while Rome burned is one of history's most famous images. Wrong instrument, wrong place.

Fiddles didn't exist in AD 64 — the violin came about 1,500 years later; Romans played the lyre. When the Great Fire started, Nero was at his villa in Antium. He rushed back, opened his gardens to the homeless and brought in food from nearby towns. The story that he sang about the fall of Troy was, even according to the historian Tacitus, a rumour. Nero was unpopular, so it stuck.

Animated, voiced and scored in code. Narration is a synthetic (text-to-speech) voice.

title: Salieri Didn't Poison Mozart #shorts
description:
Mozart died in Vienna in 1791, aged 35, after weeks of illness. Doctors at the time blamed a fever; nobody knows exactly what it was. There's no evidence of poison.

Antonio Salieri wasn't a jealous failure either: he was the emperor's top composer, taught Beethoven, Schubert, Liszt and Mozart's own son, and the two of them even wrote a cantata together in 1785 — rediscovered in 2016. The poisoning story grew from Vienna gossip years later, then Pushkin's play and the film Amadeus.

Animated, voiced and scored in code. Narration is a synthetic (text-to-speech) voice.

title: Cinco de Mayo Isn't Mexico's Independence Day #shorts
description:
Mexico's Independence Day is September 16, marking 1810, when the fight for independence from Spain began.

Cinco de Mayo marks May 5, 1862, when Mexico's smaller army beat an invading French army — one of the best in the world — at the Battle of Puebla. France came back and took Mexico City a year later, but the victory became a symbol. In Mexico it's mostly celebrated in Puebla; it's much bigger in the United States, where Mexican American activists made it a day of pride, and advertisers later made it a party.

title: Lincoln Didn't Write the Gettysburg Address on an Envelope #shorts
description:
The story goes that Lincoln scribbled the Gettysburg Address on the back of an envelope on the train. He didn't.

He began it in Washington — the first page is on Executive Mansion paper — and kept revising it. Five handwritten copies survive, none of them on an envelope. The speech lasted about two minutes; Edward Everett, who spoke before him for two hours, later wrote that Lincoln got closer to the point in two minutes than he did in two. The train-and-brown-paper version comes from a popular 1906 story.
